notes.claim: Insulation resistance readings can differ from day to day on the same machine, and what really matters is the trend over time, showing lessening resistance.
When zero lies inside the confidence interval for a fitted slope, the true slope may be zero, meaning no real trend.
As a rule of thumb, insulation resistance halves for every 10 °C rise in temperature and doubles for every 10 °C fall, so tests are corrected to one temperature before they are compared.

sources.title: The Complete Guide to Electrical Insulation Testing
sources.quote: What really matters is the trend in readings over a time period, showing lessening resistance and warning of coming problems.

sources.title: Stine, Statistics 621 (Wharton), lecture 4: regression
sources.quote: When zero lies in the CI, the “true slope” may be zero – no effect.

sources.title: The Complete Guide to Electrical Insulation Testing
sources.quote: For every 10°C increase in temperature, halve the resistance; or, for every 10°C decrease, double the resistance.
